newsitem.title: JAPAN: SOCCER-JAPAN SET FOR BRAZILIAN SOCCER FIESTA.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JAPAN SET FOR BRAZILIAN SOCCER FIESTA.

text.p: The samba drums will be beating loudly at Osaka's Nagai Stadium on Wednesday night when Brazil take on Japan in the latest match of their Asian tour.
After scraping a 2-1 win over South Korea on Sunday with two goals in the last six minutes, including a Ronaldo penalty, Brazil are clearly not firing on all cylinders.
But the prospect of watching the best team in world soccer on their Nike World Tour has captured the Japanese imagination.
All 50,000 tickets for the game, which kicks off at 7 p.m. (1000 GMT), were sold within 45 minutes of going on sale. Clearly a fiesta of football is expected.
If history is anything to go by Japan face a very tough job against the boys from Brazil. Last year, South Korea lost by the only goal to the Brazilians, whereas Japan were thrashed 5-1.

Supporting Japan against the world's premier soccer nation in the run-up to next year's World Cup in France poses a dilemma for some fans since many of their J-League heroes, including midfielders Dunga of Jubilo Iwata and Cesar Sampaio of Yokohama Flugels, hail from Brazil.
Brazil exports an abundance of soccer talent and Japan is the top importer; it's now home to the largest contingent of overseas Brazilian players in the world, along with Portugal.
One third of the managers and half the foreign players in the J-League are Brazilians.
Last year's J-League champions Kashima Antlers recently clinched the first half league title with a goal by Mazinho, in a team managed by Joao Carlos under the technical direction of Zico.
Japan even occasionally imports the sons of Japanese immigrants in Brazil. Many have proved their mettle by climbing through the ranks, such as Jorge Yonashiro and Sergio Echigo.
Another "Brazilian-Japanese" player is Kazuyoshi Miura who, at the age of 15, with a pair of brilliant feet at his disposal, went to Brazil to complete his soccer education.
Kazu was a popular star at Pele's old club Santos before he came home to play for Verdy Kawasaki when the J-League began. He is currently the star striker on the national team.

The economics of the early '90s are mostly responsible for shaping the soccer scene in Japan. Clubs are currently strapped for cash as crowds have fallen to a core of support and television ratings have relegated the sport from prime time.

After a grandstand start in 1993, clubs watched helplessly as the Japanese economy spluttered. Many fans were caught up in a short-term fad. No longer flush with funds, the clubs have become more careful about how they spend their money.

According to a J-League spokesman, "We can get Brazilian players and coaches of top calibre for less money than their European counterparts and our long and deep cultural links with Brazil give us an excellent pipeline to great new talent."

There main difference between Brazilian and European players in Japan is the skill factor. The Brazilians have better individual skills and a flair for soccer, while the Europeans play a more routine team game."
European stars are now rare in Japan and most of the top players are Brazilians, though there are also many who aren't particularly good."
So how much help will the infusion of Brazilian soccer talent be to the growth of the game in Japan?

Jonathan Spink, an executive at Jupiter Programming, a company responsible for beaming live televised soccer to Japanese viewers through cable and satellite, feels that the Brazilian influence is good for Japanese soccer.
"Currently Japan does not have enough top-class local talent to be stifled by foreign competition and if you play with the best players your standards can only rise."
Brazil's soccer talent will be in even greater demand since the J-League plans to expand with the formation of a second division.

There's likely to be a premier division of 16 teams with promotion and relegation to and from a second division of 10-16 teams, even though many critics claiming the expansion is far too much too soon.

Japan has already lost some top Brazilian players looking for a higher profile back home in their bid for a place in the World Cup squad. It's no secret that manager Mario Zagallo favours players in top flight football.
Last year, Leonardo was the first to leave the J-League, while in July Zinho quit for Palmeiras though he's promised to return to the Yokohama Flugels after the World Cup.

Cerezo Osaka lost Manoel to Botafogo, and Sampaio could also be leaving soon. The open criticism by Dunga of his teammates' lack of hard work is seen by at least one observer as a way of setting up his own exit from Japan.
